nameStory: The Eastern Copperhead gets its name from its distinctive copper-penny coloration, especially noticeable on its triangular head. When sunlight hits this snake just right, that coppery-bronze shine is unmistakable, like a newly minted penny from the U.S. Mint.
description: The Eastern Copperhead is New England's most commonly encountered venomous snake, though it's only found in the southern parts of the region. These thick-bodied pit vipers typically grow 2-3 feet long and are beautifully marked with hourglass or "Hershey's Kiss" shaped crossbands across their copper-brown bodies. Their heat-sensing pits and triangular heads immediately distinguish them from harmless snakes, and they're generally more docile than aggressive.

idTips.label: Pattern
idTips.description: Look for dark brown hourglass or bow-tie shaped crossbands that are wider at the sides and narrower across the spine, like chocolate Hershey's Kisses laid sideways across a copper-colored body

idTips.label: Head Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly triangular head that's noticeably wider than the neck, with a coppery-bronze color that feels almost metallic in sunlight

idTips.label: Scales
idTips.description: Heavily keeled scales that feel rough and ridged to the touch, giving the snake a textured, almost sandpaper-like surface

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often freezes motionless when threatened rather than fleeing, relying on camouflage - this "statue-still" behavior can lead to accidental close encounters

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Prefers rocky, wooded hillsides and stone walls where they can blend perfectly with fallen leaves and dappled sunlight

habitat: In New England, copperheads favor rocky, south-facing slopes in deciduous forests, particularly areas with stone walls, rock outcrops, and leaf litter. They're most common in Connecticut and Massachusetts, especially in hilly terrain with oak and hickory forests. You'll often find them near old stone foundations or walls where they can easily hide among the rocks and fallen leaves.

seasonality.spring: Emerge from winter dens in April-May and are often seen basking on warm rocks or stone walls during mild sunny days.
seasonality.summer: Most active during dawn and dusk hours, often hidden under logs or rocks during hot days. This is breeding season, so males may be more mobile.
seasonality.fall: Very active as they prepare for winter, often seen moving between feeding areas and winter dens. Their autumn colors blend perfectly with fallen leaves.
seasonality.winter: Enter brumation (reptile hibernation) in rock crevices or underground dens, sometimes communally with other snakes.

funFact: Baby copperheads are born with bright yellow or green tail tips that they wiggle like little worms to lure frogs and lizards within striking distance - a behavior called "caudal luring" that they lose as adults when they switch to hunting larger prey.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the harmless milk snake, but remember: "Kisses kill" - copperheads have hourglass "kiss" shapes that touch the belly scales, while milk snake bands go all the way around the body. Copperheads also have that distinctive triangular head and copper coloring that milk snakes lack.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being venomous, copperhead bites are rarely fatal to humans and they're actually quite docile - most bites occur when people accidentally step on them or try to handle them. They're an important part of the ecosystem, controlling rodent populations.
compareHints: Copperheads are the only species in their genus found in New England. Compared to other vipers like timber rattlesnakes, copperheads lack the rattle and have those distinctive hourglass crossbands rather than the chevron patterns of rattlers. They're also generally smaller and more copper-colored than the gray-brown timber rattlesnakes.
